01 — About the park

Almost a century of protected forest.

A mixed conifer and beech reserve on the southern Alpine foothills. In October 2024, 310 mm of rain in 48 hours triggered landslides that cut 38 km of trails, destroyed four bridges and damaged 220 ha of forest.

Cima Serena ridge · 2,410 mPark boundary, east
Founded
1928

97 years as a protected park, managed by the Val Serena Park Trust.

Total area
4,820ha

Of which 220 ha were damaged by the storm and landslides.

Annual visitors · 2023
420k

Before the storm. Today 60% of the park remains closed.

Location
46.3°N
11.8°E

Val Serena valley, Southern Alpine foothills · 90 min from the nearest international airport

02 — The vision · Trails & waterways

Reconnected — and ready for the next storm.

The restored park welcomes visitors across its full length, with infrastructure designed around water rather than against it: raised boardwalks, rerouted paths, living slope stabilisation and re-naturalised stream corridors.

Trails rebuilt
38km

Raised boardwalks through flood zones; paths moved off unstable slopes.

New timber bridges
4

Local larch, wider spans, elevated decks that let high water pass beneath.

Val Serena Forest Park

03 — The vision · Forest & visitors

A forest that grows back stronger.

Beyond repair: a climate-resilient mixed forest of fir, larch, beech and sycamore, plus new low-impact ways for visitors to experience it — a canopy walk, three viewpoints and a lakeside pavilion.

Lakeside visitor garden & pavilionConcept view
Trees planted
180k

Native species over 220 ha, with a five-year care programme.

Wetland habitat
+40%

Target increase; monitoring stations for birds, amphibians and soil.

05 — Roadmap 2025–2028

Sequenced over three years.

Each investment area builds on the one before it — stabilise the slopes, then rebuild the trails and replant the forest, then reopen to visitors. Monitoring runs in parallel throughout.

Year 1 · Stabilise
2025

Slopes & drainage stabilisation — 12 landslide scars secured and wetland retention basins built before work moves uphill.

Year 2 · Rebuild & replant
2026–27

Trails & bridges alongside reforestation — 38 km of paths, 4 timber bridges and 180,000 native trees.

Year 3 · Reopen
2028

Visitor facilities and full reopening — pavilion, canopy walk and three viewpoints; 420k visitors welcomed back.

06 — Risks & mitigation

The risks we are planning for.

Large-scale restoration carries real exposure — weather, funding, cost and habitat. Each one has a specific control already written into the plan, and Year 1 is funded and self-contained whatever else moves.

Monitoring & education, 5% of the budget, tracks every one of these from the first season.

Weather · slope works
+20%

Extra weather days built into the Year 1 programme. Temporary check dams hold part-worked slopes, and heavy earthworks run in the drier April–October window.

Private funding · timing
€1.9M

€4.5 M of the €6.4 M total is still being sought. The €1.9 M secured fully funds Year 1; later phases are gated to confirmed commitments.

Cost overrun · trails & bridges
+10%

Contingency ring-fenced against the €2.1 M trails-and-bridges phase. Fixed-price local larch and off-site bridge prefabrication cap the exposure.

Habitat · reforestation
220ha

Replanted in staged blocks outside the March–July nesting season. Deadwood and wildlife corridors are kept, with an ecologist signing off each block.
